title: The fan from home
hookLine: in Sri Lanka Faxian sees a merchant offer a Chinese fan and weeps with homesickness

cards: A white silk fan. That's all it is. A merchant steps up to a great image of the Buddha in a monastery in Sri Lanka and lays it down as an offering.
Nobody around him would look twice. But a Chinese monk standing beside the image looks, and keeps looking. The fan is from China, something from home after years away.
And the man who crossed a desert marked by bones, who climbed passes of snow, starts to cry.

teach.b: First, how he got there. After his years of study in India, Faxian took ship to Sri Lanka, the island on the southern road, and stayed there to find more texts.
In one monastery stood a large image of the Buddha in green jade. Second, what he wrote. In Legge's translation, Faxian describes his state of mind before the fan.
Many years had passed since he left China. The people around him were all from other lands. His eyes had not rested on a familiar hill or river, plant or tree.
His companions were gone, some dead, some scattered.
He was alone, and sadness stayed with him. Third, the moment.
By the image he saw the merchant offer a white silk fan from China, and tears filled his eyes and fell. That's the whole scene.
He doesn't explain it away; he just sets it down in his record. Fourth, why it matters that he wrote it. Faxian was a monk on a serious errand, a man trained in letting go.

And here he is, undone by a fan, and he leaves the moment in. Buddhist teaching speaks plainly about attachment and the pain of separation from what we love. Faxian's page doesn't argue with that teaching.
It shows what it can look like from the inside, in a temple, far from home, holding nothing but his own sorrow. And then, the record says, he went on with his work.

how: Buddhist pilgrims and monks who travel far to study often keep in touch with home through letters, offerings and small gifts, and travelers' records like Faxian's are read as part of the tradition's history.

o: a vow that ties a monk to one monastery
a love of travel that keeps a monk walking
clinging, and the pain of parting from what we love

practice: Bring to mind someone who lives a long way from where they started: a neighbor who moved countries, a coworker, a grandparent, maybe you.
Picture one small thing from their home that might catch them off guard, a smell, a song, a food, and on each out-breath send them a little warmth. If you pray, you can hold them in your prayer.

wordCard.voice: Attachment. The pain of separation from what we love, which Faxian's tears over a fan from home let readers see from the inside.

carryVoice: Your line: a fan from home. Even a seasoned walker can be undone by something small. Day nine hundred six, done.
